claims.claim_text: Altium's intended workflow places all part, supplier and fit/no-fit data in the schematic and propagates it forward to generated bills of materials; partial adoption of the method yields none of its benefit.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you commit 100% to do it that way, it doesn't work
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: An OutJob is a scripted output definition that produces identical manufacturing file sets across projects, making fabrication output reproducible.
claims.quote_verbatim: it generates exactly the same format files every time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because output is scripted, a misconfigured OutJob fails silently: one exported two layers of a four-layer board without error.
claims.quote_verbatim: it took us a while to figure out that he screwed up his out job
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium renders internal plane layers as negative images, which some fabricators reject; the workaround is to implement inner planes as flooded signal layers instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you do it as a plane in Altium, then it produces an inverse image
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: KiCad generates positive images for plane layers, so the same fabricator issue does not arise.
claims.quote_verbatim: I used KiCad and it generates positive, uh, images
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium's board outline layer differs from other tools' conception of an outline and is typically not contiguous, which fabricators must accommodate.
claims.quote_verbatim: their outline layers are actually typically not actually contiguous
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Schematic and PCB differencing is built into the tool and highlights changes, which is presented as the requirement for version control on hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium have their own built-in diff things
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: Files created in newer versions can be opened in older versions, a property described as essential for professional PCB work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually pull in newer versions into older software
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The file format proved robust across unstable daily builds, with no corruption of saved work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would never break it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium supports several incompatible approaches to library management and never settled on one, leaving the choice to each user group.
claims.quote_verbatim: there were multiple ways to do libraries
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium and KiCad both decouple symbol, footprint and 3D model, in contrast to an atomic model that binds them to a single manufacturer part number.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Altium or the KiCad way of doing it where they're decoupled from one another
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The panelisation tool works but is imprecise enough that manual copy-paste is often preferred.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a little janky
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Manual copy-paste panelisation is used in preference to the built-in tool even when the tool is licensed.
claims.quote_verbatim: even though I've got the panelization tool, I'm not going to do it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Keyboard shortcuts and commands were preserved from the 1985 DOS-era Protel releases for roughly three decades.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's the same since 1985 DOS version. I am not kidding.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Argues the decisive property of an EDA package is switching cost: adoption is effectively a ten-year commitment because the existing design corpus is locked into the format, and vendors are aware of this.
claims.quote_verbatim: the transaction cost of switching away from it is super high
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Arduino, IndiGoGo and Hack-a-Day - Doodad Dealer Dancing

claims.claim_text: Characterises EDA tool choice as a matter of allegiance rather than evaluation, and attempts to convert users as unproductive.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's choosing a religion
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Abandoned advocating tool changes, on the grounds that the decision is made on willingness to pay rather than features.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've just kind of given up on converting people because it's not worth it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart

claims.claim_text: Holds that tool changes require an external trigger such as leaving a job and its licence, and notes the circularity of learning a tool speculatively to win contracts that require it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Unless you have some kind of change agent in your life
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Describes migrating to Altium when Eagle moved to subscription licensing and Altium halved its price to capture the displaced users.
claims.quote_verbatim: they cut the price of Altium basically in half
claims.speaker: Charles Alexanian

claims.claim_text: Declines to buy a licence at five to six thousand dollars, having ceased daily layout work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not going to go out and pay five, six grand for Altium
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: States he will not purchase a full licence because he does not need one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I won't buy a full Altium license. I don't need it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Sets board complexity as the test, holding that Raspberry Pi-class designs do not require the tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: then it's like, meh, like you don't need Altium
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Reports pricing of roughly 5,000 dollars initially with 1,500 to 2,000 dollars annually for maintenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: 5,000 the first time, 2,000 a year after that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Justifies the cost by billable time, having migrated from Eagle when fighting the tool began consuming hours; a single day of output-generation trouble avoided repays the difference.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm spending a lot of time fighting Eagle
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: Notes the licence is unaffordable without an employer, and frames open-source alternatives as an accessibility requirement.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I, if I didn't work at a company, I probably wouldn't be able to afford to buy it
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar

claims.claim_text: Holds that KiCad is not yet a professional-grade tool and remains far from challenging Altium in high-end PCB work.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's still not a pro-level tool
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Responds that the assessment rests on outdated familiarity, while allowing it may have been correct when formed.
claims.quote_verbatim: Dave's working from old knowledge
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Estimates market share at roughly 30 percent Altium and 25 percent Eagle, with KiCad, OrCAD and Allegro near 15 percent each.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium is probably like 30%. Eagle is probably like 25%
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Segments the market by company size: larger and older firms run Cadence, while Altium holds the small and medium segment.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium really has that, that small and medium size company segment
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Describes Altium as effectively the only option for small consumer-hardware companies.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're a small company and consumer, it's like, yeah. Okay. Altium is it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Characterises the competitive landscape as Altium and everyone else.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's Altium and everyone else
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Notes Altium's decades-long dominance of Australian student licensing, and the resulting cost problem when hiring.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium just practically owns the student thing here
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: Argues the modular-block and all-FPGA vision failed because engineering does not compose that way.
claims.quote_verbatim: Everything's going to be modular block design. You'll never have to lay out boards anymore.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Credits the same FPGA toolchain as technically effective at a high level, being vendor-agnostic with drag-in processor cores and C-to-HDL synthesis, while failing on serious projects.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could drag in a processor core and it would just work
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Describes uniformly high technical staff quality at Altium, in contrast to previous employers.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've never worked at a company where everyone there knew what they were doing
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: Characterises the founder's approach as running the company as a hobby rather than to maximise returns.
claims.quote_verbatim: he didn't really care if it made huge amounts of money
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: Concurs, describing the company as a publicly traded hobby.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is a publicly traded hobby
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: States a loss of interest in the company after fourteen years of commentary.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't care that much about the Autium system anymore
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Version-locked Altium 12 for the duration of the Steam Controller project, importing a semiconductor-industry practice of freezing tool versions across long programmes to prevent CAD defects from disrupting schedule.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're going to settle on Altium 12
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Reports that the Altium 17/18 interface overhaul destroyed accumulated expertise, describing the experience of returning to a tool as a former expert and being ineffective.
claims.quote_verbatim: being an expert in a tool
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Judges much of the interface change unjustified, and questions the aggregate productivity cost to established users.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the change seemed unnecessary
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Learned of the relocation to China, and his own redundancy, when handed his final pay.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't know Altium were moving to China until they handed over my paycheck
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jason Kridner - Bonafide BeagleBoard Bionomics

claims.claim_text: Notes shares fell to ten cents during his employment, a position that would later have been worth 13.7 million dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: I could have made $13.7 million
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Altium was founded in Tasmania in 1985 by Nick Martin as Protel.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were founded in Tasmania, of all places, the Map of Tassie, in 1985 by Nick Martin
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Protel 99 SE remained the industry standard for around twenty years and was near-universal in Chinese development houses, to the point that satisfied users would not buy upgrades.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was incredibly difficult for the salespeople to sell new licenses
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The Altium name followed a merger of the internally competing Protel and PCAD products, combining PCAD's PCB strengths with Protel's schematic strengths, and was a rebranding of the company in the early 2000s.
claims.quote_verbatim: Protel eventually became Altium
claims.speaker: Matt Berggren

claims.claim_text: The name itself came from a trademark portfolio acquired with IBM-originated technology, chosen because the trademark was already owned.
claims.quote_verbatim: no one knows what it means, but they went, I like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent's New Name, Molex's New Owner and PCB artwork - Nonsensical Naming Neolatry

claims.claim_text: Founder Nick Martin was removed by the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: He was just booted out by the board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Open Source RC & Modelsource - Facinorous Financial Foulness

claims.claim_text: The successor strategy was a return to core EDA functionality and away from Internet of Things work.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are getting back into core, in quote marks, core EDA functionality
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: SpaceX, Enclosures & Startups - Urging Unemployment Ullagone

claims.claim_text: The 2014 relocation to San Diego was accompanied by an admission that the Internet of Things strategy had failed, and followed an earlier unsuccessful move to San Jose in the 1990s; US military business was reported lost over China-based R&D.
claims.quote_verbatim: they came back to Sydney with their tail between their legs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: Predicted CircuitMaker would fail, the free tool being cloud-only with no local file saving.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can't help but think it's more likely to fail than not
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Last Minute Decisions - Obdurate Onepercenter Obstacles

claims.claim_text: Declined to adopt CircuitMaker, citing KiCad as a permanently free alternative.
claims.quote_verbatim: I will not be switching
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Last Minute Decisions - Obdurate Onepercenter Obstacles

claims.claim_text: Identified the abandonment risk in a free cloud tool with no revenue model.
claims.quote_verbatim: what's to stop the board of directors just going, no, let's just scrap this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: Rates Circuit Studio good value at its price point while noting deliberate incompatibility with Altium Designer to prevent firms substituting cheap seats.
claims.quote_verbatim: They want to make it as hard as possible.
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: Reports Altium publicly signalling willingness to be acquired, with long-standing unfixed defects cited as the one argued benefit of an Autodesk takeover.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium's famously had the same bugs for 20 years
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The company was acquired at 68 dollars per share, an increase deflated against a float price of a few dollars roughly 24 years earlier.
claims.quote_verbatim: 24 years later is not a big increase
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Noted that acquisitions of this kind are frequently blocked by regulators.
claims.quote_verbatim: This kind of stuff gets blocked by regulators all the time, man.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Reports that Altium delayed a product launch after a critical video, revising its direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: they went, yeah, we're probably not quite on the right track. So, they held off.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Travel Recaps and Altium Announcements - Artisinal Aussie Assemblage

claims.claim_text: States he no longer receives a licence from the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: Altium don't want to give me a. Freaking license anymore.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
